Presidential Gubernatorial Former Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF), Michael Aondoakaa
The Federal High Court in Abuja has dismissed a suit filed by four Benue State indigenes seeking to stop former Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF), Michael Aondoakaa, from contesting the 2027 governorship election in the state.
In her judgement on Monday, Justice Joyce Abdulmalik held that the plaintiffs lacked the locus standi, or legal right, to institute the action.
The judge upheld the preliminary objection filed by the defendants, ruling that the suit was statute-barred and amounted to a pre-election matter presented as an action to enforce an earlier judgement.
She held that the suit was filed outside the mandatory 14-day period prescribed by law.
She also rejected the plaintiffs’ argument that they only became aware of Mr Aondoakaa’s nomination by the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) on 30 August.
“The evidence before the court clearly showed that the third defendant was declared the winner on June 24, 2026, and presented with a certificate of return on June 26, 2026.
“This suit, having been filed outside the mandatory 14 days, is statute-barred and is dismissed in its entirety,” the judge said.

According to the Nigerian Tribune, which reported the judgement on Monday, the court also held that the plaintiffs had failed to establish the legal basis for the reliefs they sought.
The plaintiffs, David Ejembi, Aondoaver Teryila, Joseph Okpanachi and Benedict Orkume, filed the suit, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/2152/2026, against the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), the PDP and Mr Aondoakaa.
They relied on a Supreme Court judgement in Michael Kaase Aondoakaa v. Obot (2022) 5 NWLR (Pt. 1824) 523, which they argued had barred the former AGF from holding public office.
They asked the court to declare that INEC was constitutionally bound to enforce the Supreme Court judgement by preventing the PDP from sponsoring Mr Aondoakaa in the 2027 governorship election.
They also sought an order compelling the PDP to withdraw his candidature and injunctions restraining INEC from accepting his sponsorship and Mr Aondoakaa from contesting the election.
The plaintiffs argued that sections 235 and 287(1) of the Constitution, read alongside the definition of a public office of a state in section 318(1), required the electoral commission and the PDP to comply with the apex court’s judgement.
However, Justice Abdulmalik held that the plaintiffs, who described themselves as registered voters in Benue, could not establish the standing required to pursue the action as a public interest matter.
She further held that the suit was, in substance, a pre-election matter.
Since the plaintiffs were not aspirants in the PDP governorship primary, they lacked the legal standing to challenge its outcome.
The judge also noted that they were not parties to the earlier case they sought to enforce and had not presented sufficient material evidence to justify the reliefs.
Mr Aondoakaa’s legal team, led by Anthony Ijohor, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), urged the court to dismiss the suit as incompetent.
The defence challenged the plaintiffs’ counter-affidavit, arguing that some of its paragraphs amounted to documentary hearsay because the information was attributed to a lawyer in the same firm rather than someone with first-hand knowledge of the facts.
It also argued that the plaintiffs could not use a fresh action to enforce a final judgement in a case to which they were not parties.
The defence maintained that only a judgement creditor could ordinarily seek enforcement against a judgement debtor. It cited previous court decisions, including AMCON v. Capital Oil & Gas (2019), in support of its position.
It further argued that the suit was premature because the 2027 election had not been held and that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated any special interest or injury arising from Mr Aondoakaa’s candidature.
The defence also maintained that the grounds for disqualification from an election were set out in section 182 of the Constitution and that the plaintiffs could not compel INEC to prevent the PDP from sponsoring a candidate based on their claims.
The suit arose from a Supreme Court judgement affirming Mr Aondoakaa’s disqualification from holding public office over his conduct while serving as Attorney-General of the Federation.
The dispute originated from the 2007 PDP primary election for the Uyo Federal Constituency in Akwa Ibom State, which Emmanuel Obot won.
Mr Obot had challenged the substitution of his name with that of another candidate. Following court proceedings, the Court of Appeal ordered that a fresh election tribunal be constituted to hear his petition.
However, Mr Aondoakaa, who was then AGF, wrote to the President of the Court of Appeal, urging him not to give effect to the appellate court’s decision.
After the tribunal ruled in Mr Obot’s favour in April 2008, the Court of Appeal affirmed the decision in December 2009 and ordered INEC to issue him a certificate of return.
Mr Aondoakaa subsequently wrote to the then INEC chairman and the Speaker of the House of Representatives, asking them not to implement the judgement.
Mr Obot later instituted a separate suit challenging Mr Aondoakaa’s fitness to hold public office.
On 1 June 2010, the Federal High Court ruled that Mr Aondoakaa was not a competent, fit and proper person to hold public office and awarded Mr Obot ₦50 million in damages.
The Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Aondoakaa’s appeal on 3 September 2015, affirming the lower court’s decision.
On 10 December 2021, the Supreme Court also dismissed his appeal, affirming the decisions of the two lower courts.
In its judgement, the apex court criticised his conduct while serving as the country’s chief law officer, holding that he had acted in a manner unbecoming of the office.
PREMIUM TIMES reported on 21 September that four Benue indigenes had filed a fresh suit seeking to stop Mr Aondoakaa from contesting the 2027 governorship election, relying on the Supreme Court judgment.
Mr Aondoakaa’s political moves have also drawn attention ahead of the 2027 election.
PREMIUM TIMES reported on 30 March that the former AGF had resigned from the All Progressives Congress (APC), where he was a leading governorship aspirant in Benue.
In a statement announcing his resignation, he said the decision followed consultations with his family, political associates and supporters.
He also expressed appreciation to President Bola Tinubu and the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, George Akume.
Mr Aondoakaa did not disclose his next political destination at the time. He later emerged as the PDP’s governorship candidate for the 2027 election.
He had previously contested the APC governorship primary in 2022 but lost to the party’s eventual candidate, Hyacinth Alia, who went on to win the 2023 governorship election.
The latest judgement dismisses the suit brought by the four indigenes.
The court’s decision was based on the plaintiffs’ lack of legal standing and the procedural defects identified in the action.
